text: After yesterday’s call, I want to be clear about what we agreed. The buyer intends to keep the brand for at least two years. They insisted on keeping me as CEO until the end of the transition. We refused to sign the exclusivity clause in its current form. We agreed to postpone the price discussion until the audit is finished. Please remember to send the updated numbers to their team by Friday.

When I ask a founder what happens after the sale, the answer I trust is the precise one. A founder who says I intend to stay for two years, and I have already stopped running sales myself, has given me two facts. A founder who says I will try to stay has told me he is not sure. Try is a small word, and in a negotiation it costs money. So I always ask the same follow-up question: what have you already stopped doing?

I remember signing the letter of intent and feeling that the hard part was over. It was not. I forgot to ask what the buyer expected me to keep doing, and I had promised to stay without asking what staying meant. If I did it again, I would insist on writing it down: which decisions I keep, which ones I stop making, and the date I stop making them.
